How to Beat Procrastination Like It Owes You Money
Inaction is primarily an emotional problem rather than a lack of knowledge or discipline.
By setting up an environment that makes desired actions inevitable and using small, concrete steps, you can overcome procrastination and build momentum.
Counted in visits instead of years, the time left with the people you love is smaller than it feels.
Twenty minutes, no experience needed: breath first, then the basic shapes, at an easy pace you can repeat every morning.
When you feel stuck, identify the smallest, simplest action you can take today to move toward your goal and do it immediately to trigger the do something principle.
Call your parents this week, and put the next visit on the calendar.
Tomorrow morning, try the two-stage pour with a 45-second bloom.
Choose what you will leave undone this week, on purpose.
Start the trail down from the Golgo plateau early: it takes about an hour.
Swipe left on a task that isn’t for you.
All done. New tasks arrive with your saves.

Six saves this week, and the loudest one is a video on procrastination. Mark Manson’s point: putting things off is a feeling, not a lack of know-how, and the way out is the smallest step you can take today.

Four Thousand Weeks says you will never get to everything, so choose. The Tail End puts a number on why it matters: the visits you have left with your parents. And a quiet film, a slow coffee and a hidden beach make the case for doing fewer things, properly.
Manson says action comes before motivation, not after it. Burkeman and The Tail End add the reason not to wait: the time is shorter than it feels.
